t: Begun in 447 BCE in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persians, it was completed in 438 BCE, with work on its decoration continuing until 432 BCE, and also served as a treasury.
It was in turn a temple of Athena, a church of the Virgin Mary and a mosque, until a Venetian mortar round blew up the Ottoman gunpowder magazine inside it in 1687.
Agents of the 7th Earl of Elgin removed about half its surviving sculptures; in 1983 Greece formally asked for the return of those in the British Museum, which has consistently refused.
dyk: Every statue on the west pediment has a fully completed back, which no one could have seen once the sculpture was in place on the temple.
ev: The Persians sack Athens and raze the Acropolis while the Older Parthenon is still under construction
The architects Ictinos and Callicrates begin the present temple in the building project of Pericles
Theodosius II decrees that all pagan temples in the Eastern Roman Empire be closed
The emperor Basil II goes on pilgrimage to Athens for the sole purpose of worshipping at the Parthenon, then a church of the Virgin Mary
After the Ottoman conquest of Athens the Parthenon becomes a mosque, its tower extended into a minaret
During the Morean War a Venetian mortar round blows up the Ottoman gunpowder magazine in the Parthenon, wrecking its central part
Agents of Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, remove about half the surviving sculptures and send them to Britain
The Greek government sets up the Committee for the Conservation of the Acropolis Monuments to preserve and restore the buildings

f.made: Built for Athens in the building project of Pericles; the sculptor Phidias had general supervision and charge of its sculptural decoration; the architects Ictinos and Callicrates; marble workers, carpenters, metalworkers and labourers, slaves and foreigners working beside citizens for the same pay
f.form: An octastyle peripteral Doric temple of Pentelic marble, with eight columns at each end and seventeen on each side, a two-chambered cella, an Ionic frieze, 92 metopes and two sculpted pediments; its cella once held Phidias’ chryselephantine statue of Athena Parthenos
f.where: Standing, much damaged and under restoration, on the Acropolis of Athens; most surviving sculptures are in the Acropolis Museum in Athens and the British Museum in London, others in the Louvre, the National Museum of Denmark and the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna
f.known: its Doric architecture and optical refinements; the Ionic frieze, often read as the Panathenaic procession; the metopes and pediments; the lost statue of Athena Parthenos; the explosion of 1687; the dispute over the sculptures removed by Elgin; its standing as a symbol of ancient Greece, Western civilisation and democracy
